chapter_theme: Sulking and its right measure. The quarrel is salt: just enough makes love tasty and a little more spoils it. Nothing holds it in check except that the other person cares, as the chapter's closing verses, in which the man finds her sulk has gone too far, make clear.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar has the friend tease and advise (1301-1302), the woman send the man back to the courtesans with sarcasm (1303-1304), the man reflect on sulking after making up (1305-1307), and the man again, in a sulk he can't end (1308-1310). Manakkudavar differs on 1305, 1306 and 1308.

1301.reading: The friend tells the woman not to embrace him but to sulk, so that they may watch his sharp pain for a little while.
1301.nuance: It's mischief with a purpose. Parimelazhagar says the friend has actually come as his envoy, and sides with the woman, teasing, as a way of bringing her round. சிறிது, 'a little', is the word that matters: the quarrel mustn't go on long.

1302.reading: The friend says that sulking is like the right amount of salt, and letting it go on a little too long is like a little too much salt.
1302.nuance: The image puts sulking in the kitchen, as an everyday and necessary ingredient without any drama. The second line is exact: just a little too much is enough to spoil it. Kalaignar makes the measure a time span, and Parimelazhagar makes it knowing when desire is about to fade.

1303.reading: The woman says that not embracing those who have sulked with you is like adding sharp pain to those already in distress.

positions.position: She means courtesans: go back to them, she tells the man returning from them, since they'll suffer without you. It's sarcasm.
positions.quote: நும்மைப் பெறாது புலந்தூடியிருக்கின்ற பரத்தையரைப் போய்ப் புலவி நீக்கிப் புல்லீராயின், அவராற்றார்

positions.position: It's a general truth about lovers: leaving a sulking partner unreconciled is cruel.

1304.reading: The woman says that not reconciling those who have sulked is like cutting a withered creeper at its root.

positions.position: She again means the other women, and she adds that she has no right to sulk, since she has their sons to look at; so go to them.
It's about any partner who stays aloof from a sulking lover.

1305.reading: The grace of those good in their virtues is the depth of sulking in flower-eyed women; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.

positions.position: The man, reconciled, reflects to himself that even faultless men find this sulking lovely.
positions.quote: தலைமகளைப் புலவி நீக்கிக் கூடிய தலைமகன் தன்னுள்ளே சொல்லியது.

positions.position: The friend tells the woman that sulking suits courtesans, and that she shouldn't sulk at those not worth it.
positions.quote: இது பரத்தையரோடு புலந்து கூறிய தலைமகட்குத் தோழி கூறியது.

1306.reading: Without serious and light quarrels, love is like over-ripe fruit and unripe fruit; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
1306.nuance: There are two kinds of quarrels for two kinds of failure, and the verse uses them in order: no deep quarrel, and love is fruit going off; no light quarrel, and love is unripe. Manakkudavar supplies the tastes, sour and astringent. Pope's couplet reads 'ripened fruit' as a good thing, and the commentators don't.

positions.position: The man praises both kinds of quarrel after making up.
The woman speaks, saying that there is some good in the sulking that is then healed.
positions.quote: இஃது உணர்தற்கு நல்லது உளதென்று தலைமகள் கூறியது.

1307.reading: The man says there is one pain even within sulking: the worry about whether union will be delayed or not.
1307.nuance: This is where the game has its risk. Parimelazhagar takes it as the worry that union will be put off, and Kalaignar as a worry that the time for union will shrink. In either case, the player can't be sure the quarrel will end in time.

1308.reading: What use is it to suffer, when there is no lover who knows that this person is suffering? The speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar, and the friend, speaking to him, for Manakkudavar.

positions.position: The man is himself sulking, because she won't yield to his pleading.
positions.quote: இவள் நம் காதலியல்லள்; அன்மையின், இந்நோவு அறியாள்

positions.position: The friend tells the man this when she has come inside, knowing about his sulking.
positions.quote: அதனை யறிந்து அகம்புக்க தோழி அவனுக்குச் சொல்லியது.

1309.reading: The man says water is sweet in the shade, and sulking too is sweet only with those who love.
1309.nuance: It's a reciprocal theory of sulking. A quarrel is a pleasure only inside a shared love, and without it there is only heat. Parimelazhagar applies this pointedly: she doesn't feel this for him, and so her sulk is unpleasant.

1310.reading: The man, in Parimelazhagar's reading, says that his heart's wish to join with someone who leaves a sulk to wither is simply craving.
1310.nuance: அவா, 'craving', is a strong word to use on one's own heart, with a long negative history in the Kural's ethics. He diagnoses himself exactly as the ascetic chapter might, and it doesn't stop him.

links.note: உப்பு is the word in both. In 1302 the salt is the sulk, measured carefully. In 1328 the salt is the sweetness of the union that follows, as Parimelazhagar glosses it. The cook's image runs through both chapters, with the same word for the seasoning and the taste.

1191 calls requited love the stoneless fruit, the ideal of enjoyment with nothing in the way. 1306 says love without quarrels is fruit gone bad or not yet ripe. So the obstacle that 1191 wishes away, 1306 says is what makes the fruit ripe.

366 warns the renunciant to fear craving (அவா), because it deceives. In 1310, the sulking man names the same craving as what drives his heart to her. He uses the moral vocabulary correctly, with no intention of following it.

source_issues: 1305: Kalaignar's entry ends with stray text, உ. இடைமிடை சொல்நலம் ..., editorial matter about reading the Kural that is not commentary on this verse. It was not used.
1303: Manakkudavar's entry, flagged [#], repeats Parimelazhagar's gloss.
1302: Parimelazhagar's headnote has அவர் சொல்லியது where அவள் seems intended, given the friend's voice.
